{
    "id": "17-infrastructure/alerting-design",
    "title": "Alerting Design",
    "category": "17-infrastructure",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Build alerts around user-visible symptoms and service objectives rather than raw causes, so a page means real impact and silence means real health.",
    "body": "Alerting Design Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description An alert on every metric is a pager that cannot be trusted, and a pager that cannot be trusted gets silenced — usually right before the one that mattered. This skill designs alerting from the top down: start from what users experience, define objectives with error budgets, and alert on the burn rate of those budgets. Cause-level signals become dashboards and debug entries, not pages, because a page is a claim that a human must act now, and every unactionable claim spends trust the system needs for the real ones. When to Use Use whenever a service is on call — user-facing or internal — and especially where pages have grown noisy enough that responders pre-filter them. Do not page on individual cause metrics with no user-visible symptom; a nearly full disk at three in the morning is a dashboard, not a human. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The user-visible service level being protected | | | | Yes | How fast the error budget is being consumed | | | | Yes | The signal that measures the user experience | Procedure 1. Define the objective first — what users experience, measured as availability or latency — before writing a single alert. 2. Alert on burn rate: page when the error budget would exhaust within a bounded window, not on any single bad sample. 3. Keep causes out of the pager: route saturation and dependency signals to dashboards and debug pages, not to humans. 4. Make every page actionable: name the runbook, the owner, and the first command to run, in the alert itself. 5. Review alert performance like code: page rate, action rate, and the fraction of pages that were real become metrics. 6. Retire or repair chatty alerts immediately; a noisy alert is not a safety margin, it is a removed one. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Symptom-based, budget-burning pages with runbooks | | | | Page rate, action rate, and precision over time | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Cause paging | Humans notified of every unhealthy-looking metric | Page on symptoms and budget burn, not causes | | Unactionable pages | A page with no runbook and no owner | Name the runbook and first step in the alert | | Alert fatigue | So many pages that real ones get ignored | Retire chatty alerts; measure alert precision | | Missing objectives | Alerts exist but no user experience is defined | Define the service objective before alerting on it | | Static thresholds | A fixed line that pages nightly at low traffic | Use burn-rate windows instead of single thresholds | Security and Authority Boundary Alert content travels to the widest, least protected channel in an organization — phones and chat: alert payloads must not embed credentials, internal topology details, or user data, and access to the alerting configuration itself must be protected, because silencing rules a re a prime target for an intruder who wants the quiet path. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Prometheus alerting documentation (https://prometheus.io/docs/alerting/latest/overview/). 2. The SRE Workbook chapter on alerting on service level objectives (https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/). {
    "id": "17-infrastructure/blue-green-deployment",
    "title": "Blue-Green Deployment",
    "category": "17-infrastructure",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Run two production environments and switch traffic between them, so a release becomes a reversible routing change instead of a waiting period for breakage.",
    "body": "Blue-Green Deployment Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A deployment that mutates the live environment in place makes rollback a race against the damage. This skill keeps two full environments — blue, live, and green, idle — and makes the release a routing flip: the new version deploys to the idle color, is verified there, traffic switches to it, and the old color stays warm for exactly as long as the new one needs to prove itself. Rollback is then the same switch in the other direction, which is what makes the flip a decision rather than a gamble. When to Use Use for stateless or forward-compatible services where a full second environment is affordable and a fast, reversible cutover is worth the cost. Do not blue-green around breaking database changes: if the old color cannot run on the new schema, the switch is not reversible and the pattern is theater. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The version being deployed to the idle environment | | | | Yes | The traffic control between the two environments | | | | Yes | How long the old environment stays warm after the flip | Procedure 1. Keep two environments, with the idle one always ready to receive the next release. 2. Deploy the new version to the idle color only, and verify it there — health, smoke, readiness — while production is untouched. 3. Flip routing to the new color, gradually or at once by design, and watch the user-visible symptoms rather than the deploy logs. 4. Keep the old color warm for the soak period: rollback during soak is a routing change, measured in seconds. 5. Handle state carefully: the schema and its consumers must be forward-compatible with both colors, or the flip is one-way. 6. Retire the old version after soak, and immediately prepare the idle color for the next release — the pattern only works while it is always two environments. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The flip with time, direction, and verification evidence | | | | The reverse switch, ready during the entire soak | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | In-place drift | The idle environment quietly becoming non-redeployable | Rehearse deploys to the idle color regularly | | One-way schema | A migration the old color cannot survive | Forward-compatible schema changes before the flip | | Instant retirement | The old version destroyed before the soak ends | Keep the old color warm for the full soak | | Verification in production | Testing deferred until after the flip | Verify on the idle color before switching | | Stateful split | Session state trapped on the wrong color | Externalize state or drain sessions before the flip | Security and Authority Boundary The routing switch is a security boundary: whoever can flip traffic between environments can redirect production, s o route changes require the same authorization and audit as production deploys, and the idle environment must hold production data protections even while idle. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Martin Fowler's article on blue-green deployment (https://martinfowler.com/bliki/BlueGreenDeployment.html). 2. Wikipedia's overview of blue-green deployment (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue-green_deployment). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. {
    "id": "17-infrastructure/capacity-planning",
    "title": "Capacity Planning",
    "category": "17-infrastructure",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Forecast infrastructure capacity needs from utilization trends and growth assumptions, producing headroom recommendations with stated assumptions rather than single-point guesses.",
    "body": "Capacity Planning Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Capacity planning converts utilization history into headroom decisions. The skill covers measuring current utilization at peak rather than average, projecting demand under explicit growth scenarios, deriving resource needs with target utilization ceilings, and presenting recommendations with the assumptions attached so they can be argued with. The output is a scenario table, not one number, because the honest answer depends on inputs nobody controls. When to Use Use when compute, storage, or network capacity must be provisioned ahead of expected growth, or when recurring saturation needs a structural rather than reactive fix. Do not plan from average utilization. Peaks are what break systems, and a plan sized to averages fails precisely when it matters. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Time series of utilization for each constrained resource | | | | Yes | Plausible demand scenarios with rates and event shocks | | | | Yes | Target utilization per resource that triggers scaling | Procedure 1. Measure utilization at peak windows per resource, not period averages. 2. Define growth scenarios explicitly: trend, step events, and their probabilities. 3. Project demand per scenario over the planning horizon. 4. Derive required capacity per scenario against the target ceilings. 5. Add headroom for the noisiest scenario and state the chosen margin. 6. Publish the scenario table with assumptions, trigger thresholds, and review dates. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Required capacity per resource per scenario | | | | Chosen provisioning with the margin and rationale | | | | Utilization alarms that force a plan re-run | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Average-based sizing | Averages hide the peaks that break systems | Size to observed peak windows | | Single-point forecast | One growth number treated as fact | Scenario table with assumptions stated | | No trigger thresholds | Plan goes stale until saturation hits | Utilization alarms that force a re-run | | Hidden coupling missed | One resource sized without its dependencies | Model constrained resources together | | Correlated demand shocks | Scenarios assume independent growth | Include compound worst cases in the table | Security and Authority Boundary Capacity data reveals system architecture and business growth. Treat utilization and projection artifacts as internal, avoid exposing them in shared dashboards, and provision through the same review discipline as any production change, since headroom decisions are also availability decisions. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Wikipedia article on capacity planning (https://en.wikipedi a.org/wiki/Capacity_planning). 2. The Kubernetes resource management documentation for requests and limits (https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/).     "id": "17-infrastructure/cloud-cost-optimization",
    "title": "Cloud Cost Optimization",
    "category": "17-infrastructure",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Reduce cloud spend by right-sizing resources, eliminating idle capacity, selecting pricing models, and attributing costs per service, with savings verified after every change rather than assumed.",
    "body": "Cloud Cost Optimization Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Cost optimization is an engineering loop, not a cleanup day. The skill covers attributing spend to services with allocation tags, finding waste by comparing provisioned to observed peak utilization, right-sizing with headroom rules, committing predictable steady load to reserved or committed-use pricing, and verifying each change against the bill after it lands. Savings are measured in the billing data or they are claimed nowhere. When to Use Use when cloud spend must be reduced or held flat against growth, or when bills rise without a clear attribution of the increase. Do not cut capacity without observing utilization peaks first. An oversized instance is waste; a right-sized-away headroom is an outage with a monthly line item. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Per-resource spend with service and tag attribution | | | | Yes | Observed peak utilization for provisioned resources | | | | No | Reserved and committed-use pricing available for steady load | Procedure 1. Attribute all spend to services through allocation tags before optimizing anything. 2. Find waste: resources with observed peaks far below provisioned capacity. 3. Right-size against peak utilization with an explicit headroom rule, never averages. 4. Match pricing models to load shape: commitments for steady, on-demand for spiky. 5. Schedule or automate idle capacity, such as off-hours dev environments. 6. Verify every change against the next billing cycle and record realized savings. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Spend per service and tag with anomalies flagged | | | | Changes ranked by expected savings, with headroom rationale | | | | Realized savings per change, verified against bills | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Unattributed spend | Resources without tags bill to a mystery bucket | Tag policy enforced before optimization | | Headroom cut too thin | Right-sized away the safety margin | Peak-based sizing with an explicit headroom rule | | Commitment lock-in | Steady discount bought for spiky load | Match commitment only to demonstrably steady usage | | Savings claimed, not verified | Estimates reported as wins | Verify against billing data after every change | | Optimization by deletion | Idle-looking resources that are standby capacity | Confirm purpose before removing any resource | Security and Authority Boundary Cost dashboards expose system topology and business volume. Keep attribution data internal, be careful exporting billing detail to third-party tools, and never let optimization scripts delete resources without an approval path, because some waste-shaped resources are load-bearing. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The AWS cost management services overview (https://aws.amazo n.com/aws-cost-management/). 2. {
    "id": "17-infrastructure/container-image-tagging",
    "title": "Container Image Tagging",
    "category": "17-infrastructure",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Tag container images with immutable, traceable identifiers — semantic version tags, registry digests, and build provenance — so deployments reference an exact artifact auditable after the fact.",
    "body": "Container Image Tagging Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A tag is a label someone can move; a digest is an identity they cannot. This skill pins that difference into the pipeline: builds get version tags once, deployments reference images by digest, a tag is never reassigned to different bytes, and every artifact carries build provenance — source commit, build definition, timestamp. The result is that any deployed environment can answer \"exactly which bytes are running, and where did they come from\". When to Use Use for any container image that reaches a deployment — application services, tooling images, CI runner environments. Do not deploy floating tags such as or a bare branch name; a deployment that cannot name its bytes cannot be rolled back to them either. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The image being built and tagged | | | | Yes | The release version this build belongs to | | | | Yes | The content-addressed identity from the registry | | | | Yes | Source commit, build definition, and timestamp | Procedure 1. Build once per version; the artifact from one build receives all its tags at creation time. 2. Tag with the semantic version; tags are claims about content, applied once and never retagged. 3. Record the registry digest; deployments pin by digest, with the version tag kept for humans. 4. Attach provenance to the artifact — source commit, b uild definition, build time — as metadata or attestation. 5. Reject retag requests: a tag that points at new bytes is a new version, whatever it is called. 6. Keep tag-to-digest mappings queryable so an environment's running bytes can be resolved historically. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Version tag, digest, and provenance per image | | | | The digest deployments reference | | | | Who tagged what, when, from which build | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | in production | Environments reference a moving tag | Pin deployments to digests | | Retagged versions | The same version label naming different bytes | Refuse retags; new bytes get a new version | | Tag-only references | Digest never recorded at release time | Store tag-to-digest mappings per release | | Missing provenance | Artifact cannot be traced to source or build | Attach source commit and build definition | | Cross-registry drift | The same tag resolves differently per registry | Resolve and compare digests, not tag names | Security and Authority Boundary Tagging identifies artifacts; it does not make them safe. Vulnerability scanning and signature verification are separate steps whose verdicts attach to the digest, not to the label. Evidence This skill is grou nded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Docker CLI reference for image tagging (https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/image/tag/). 2. Wikipedia's overview of immutable objects (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immutable_object). {
    "id": "17-infrastructure/database-backup-automation",
    "title": "Database Backup Automation",
    "category": "17-infrastructure",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Automate database backups with declared retention, restore verification, and encryption, treating a backup as real only after a monitored restore test proves it usable.",
    "body": "Database Backup Automation Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a backup. The skill covers scheduling full and incremental backups with a retention policy that survives audit, encrypting and off-siting them, and, decisively, restoring on a schedule into an isolated environment to verify the backup is complete, current, and usable. Every backup run reports duration, size, and integrity; every restore test reports recovery time against the recovery objectives. When to Use Use when production databases need scheduled, verifiable backups with retention and off-site copies, or when an existing backup routine has never been restore-tested. Do not declare backup coverage from successful backup jobs alone. Unrestored backups fail at the worst possible moment, usually for silent corruption or version drift reasons. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Target database with size, engine, and change rate | | | | Yes | Schedule, retention tiers, and recovery objectives | | | | Yes | Isolated environment for scheduled restore verification | Procedure 1. Define the policy: full and incremental cadence, retention tiers, and recovery time and point objectives. 2. Run backups on schedule, recording duration, size, checksum, and completion status. 3. Encrypt backups at rest and in transit, and copy them off-site per policy. 4. Prune expired backups per retention tiers an d log what was removed. 5. Restore on schedule into the isolated environment and verify completeness and usability. 6. Report measured recovery time against the objective and alert on drift. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Runs with size, duration, checksum, and status | | | | Latest restore verification with recovery time measured | | | | Backups held per tier and prune history | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Unrestorable backup discovered late | Restore never tested until needed | Scheduled restore verification in an isolated environment | | Silent corruption | Bit rot in stored backup files | Checksums on write and on restore | | Retention breach | Old backups kept or pruned wrongly | Tiered retention with prune logging and audit | | Credential exposure | Backup encryption keys mishandled | Key management separated from backup storage | | Version drift | Restore target newer or older than backup format | Test with the engine version used in production | Security and Authority Boundary Backups concentrate the entire database, so they inherit and exceed its sensitivity. Encrypt at rest and in transit, store keys separately from backups, restrict restore-environment access, and log every backup and restore operation for audit. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The PostgreSQL backup and restore documentation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/backup.html). 2.     "body": "Declarative Infrastructure Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Infrastructure described imperatively is infrastructure nobody can rebuild: the console clicks that made it exist live in a browser history.     "body": "Dependency Auditor Description Audit declared external dependencies and executable skill examples in isolated environments. The auditor records pass/fail evidence and proposes badge artifacts without directly changing canonical trust state. > Phase 3 of the Dependency Watchdog pipeline. > Closes the gap between Package Exists (🟡 Yellow) and Code Runs (🟢 Green). The Execution Gap The AST Sweep (Phase 1) confirms that a skill's declared packages exist on PyPI and are free of known CVEs. But existence ≠ execution. A package might: - Have breaking API changes in its latest release - Require a native system dependency (e.g. , ) absent from the runner - Conflict with another skill's dependencies when installed together - Simply have a typo in its import path in the code example The Dependency Auditor solves this by running the code, not just scanning it. --- Architecture --- Isolation Strategy Each skill runs in a completely independent virtual environment. This prevents dependency bleed between skills — Skill A's cannot shadow Skill B's . > Why not a single shared venv for all skills? > Because conflicts between skill deps would produce false re sults. > Skill A might pass only because Skill B's dep happened to satisfy its import. > Isolation ensures every Green badge is independently earned. --- Verdict Logic The auditor distinguishes three outcomes. The distinction between and is the single most important design decision — it keeps the CI signal clean. | Verdict | Condition | Badge Action | |---|---|---| | | Snippet exits 0, no ImportError/RuntimeError | Promote Yellow → 🟢 Green (via PR) | | | Snippet exits non-zero, or raises on import | Stays Yellow, opens issue with traceback | | | No Python snippets found, or skill has no deps declared | No badge change, not flagged as broken | --- The Human-in-the-Loop Contract The badge is not written directly into canonical skill content. A passing audit produces a proposed badge artifact on a new branch and opens a Pull Request. The exact PR HEAD is merged only when required repository CI, security, tests, and invariants pass. This is the critical security feature. Without it, a snippet that passes due to a flaky network call or a temporary PyPI outage could silently award a Green badge that isn't earned. --- Recursive Dogfooding This skill ( ) is itself subject to the badge pipeline it describes. - Its own and imports are scanned by the AST Sweep → Yellow badge - The Dependency Auditor runs its own snippets in an isolated venv - If they pass → a verification PR is opened → exact-head repository CI gates the merge → Green badge The tool that audits the repository is itself audited by the repository. This is the self-healing property of the infrastructure. --- Security: Network Constraint Model > See for the full threat model. The short version: | Risk Level | Scenario | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Low (current) | Trusted contributor PRs, reviewed before merge | Ephemeral GH runner (discarded after job) | | Medium (community PRs) | Unreviewed code execution in audit | Require maintainer approval before audit workflow runs | | High (if abuse detected) | Adversarial snippet exfiltration | Docker container for execution | For the current scope — a curated, maintainer-reviewed repository — the ephemeral runner model is the primary and sufficient containment strategy. --- Failure Modes - Verdict overreach: recording pass/fail evidence as a trust judgment; the auditor records evidence and proposes badges, it does not change canonical trust state. - Isolation leakage: network or filesystem egress from the audit environment beyond the documented constraint model invalidates that run's evidence. - Pinned-evidence drift: verdicts referencing dependency versions that no longer match the resolved lockfile at audit time; record the exact resolved versions. - Transitive blind spots: auditing declared dependencies only while the exploitable surface lives in transitive or undeclared (phantom) dependencies. - Stale advisories: advisory databases with lagging or missing entries producing false \"no known issues\" verdicts; record advisory database version and freshness. The skill covers expressing records as versioned configuration, choosing TTLs deliberately as a trade between change speed and resolver load, pre-validating changes against the existing zone, applying with a rollback plan, and verifying propagation from independent resolvers rather than assuming it.     "body": "Secrets Management Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A credential in a config file is a credential in a repository, a backup, and a log shipper forever. This skill routes around that: secrets live in a dedicated store, workloads fetch them at start time under an authenticated identity, each credential carries a scope and a lease, and rotation is routine rather than an incident. The audit trail closes the loop — who fetched what, when, under which role — because the question after a leak is never only what got out, but what it could reach and for how long. When to Use Use for any credential a workload needs — API keys, database credentials, signing material — delivered at runtime by identity, with rotation intervals that limit the lifetime of a stolen value. Do not build home-grown encryption schemes or stash credentials in environment files that outlive their leak; the managed path exists precisely so the shortcuts do not have to. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The logical name the workload requests | | | | Yes | The authenticated workload identity making the request | | | | Yes | Scope, duration, and renewal policy for the grant | Procedure 1. Inventory the credentials first: every secret gets an owner, a scope, and a rotation interval before it gets a store entry. 2. Store values only in the secrets system, addressed by logical name, with no copies in code, config files, or CI variables. 3. Deliv er at runtime: the workload authenticates as itself and receives only the entries its scope allows. 4. Lease and rotate: credentials expire by policy, and rotation is a routine operation with a tested procedure, not an emergency. 5. Audit every fetch — identity, secret, time — and route the log somewhere a compromised workload cannot edit. 6. Revoke on suspicion, and drill revocation like backups: a rotation path never exercised will fail exactly when it matters.
